p.6 states 'CMLN money mules may also engage in "smurfing" operations across multiple depository institution branches to deposit illicit funds' and notes mules deposit large cash sums 'irrespective of Currency Transaction Reporting requirements' -- classic sub-CTR structuring, footnoted at p.6 (fn.35) as teams structuring transactions to evade CTR filing.

emergent_label: Chinese Underground Banking Mirror Transactions (IVTS)
rationale: p.3 and p.5 develop a dedicated 'CMLNs' Use of Mirror Transactions' mechanism: a U.S.-based CMLN receives Cartel USD while a Mexico-based CMLN counterpart simultaneously pays an equivalent peso amount into the Cartel's Mexico accounts (or the reverse leg with a China-based operator settling in RMB), so value moves globally without any cross-border transfer of the underlying cash -- a Chinese-underground-banking / IVTS book-balancing technique, also usable via CVC. Search for 'mirror transaction black market peso exchange' and 'underground banking currency control evasion' returned only weak, non-substantive matches (best 0.42), so proposed as emergent.

Core, extensively developed theme of the alert: DPs transfer shareholdings to trusted proxies (p.3), divest below the 50% control threshold (p.4, p.10), and use nominee directors/shareholders and family/associate transfers to conceal continued control (p.10-11).

Indicator 4 (p.10) describes trust arrangements and complex offshore corporate structures, including circular ownership, shell companies and trust structures used to obscure whether the original owner retains control, matching the doctrine's structural-opacity mechanism.

Page 4 describes DPs and Russian money launderers exploring crypto-asset payment channels, including cash-to-crypto services able to move significant volumes, specifically to circumvent sanctions and reduced SWIFT access.

Single bullet on p.12 (indicator 34) flags 'Circumvention attempts through Open Account Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) typology, such as increases in third party open account payments' as a suspicious-payment indicator; not otherwise developed in the narrative.

Enabler-detection indicators on p.11 describe numerous share transfers between corporations incorporated by the same people and sharing a registered address, and large numbers of off-the-shelf corporations with no trading record used as throughputs -- classic shell-company-network markers.

Advisory devotes a full section to Iran's 'shadow fleet' (p.4): old, poorly maintained, uninsured/underinsured vessels; frequent renaming, reflagging and false-flagging; AIS manipulation, ship-to-ship transfers and cargo relabeling as 'Malaysian blend' to disguise origin (p.4). Dedicated red flags on vessel name/flag/IMO manipulation and AIS/STS irregularities follow at p.8, matching SAN002 indicators directly (renaming, flag changes, AIS gaps, ship-to-ship transfers, free trade zones, Iranian petroleum).

Front companies are the connective tissue of the entire scheme: p.3 describes front companies in third-country free trade zones layering transactions; p.5 describes exchange houses managing 'numerous front companies' with no web presence, minimal substance, and falsified invoices; p.6 case study shows the Zarringhalam network operating a 'sprawling network of front companies' in UAE/Hong Kong; p.7 shows Sahara Thunder as MODAFL's main front company; p.9 red flags list opaque ownership, obscure controllers, residential/co-located addresses and shared counterparties/addresses/owners as front-company indicators, directly matching SAN004's indicator set.

A dedicated 'Weapons Procurement Efforts' section (p.6-7) describes Iran seeking foreign-produced weapons components, dual-use goods and chemicals for its ballistic missile/UAV programs, evading U.S. export controls via procurement agents, transaction layering, falsified documentation and transshipment through third countries (China/Hong Kong, Turkiye, Southeast Asia). The Sahara Thunder case study (p.7) and the weapons-procurement red flags (p.9, e.g. customers transacting with technology companies/chemical suppliers, funds flowing from commodities traders to electronics suppliers) match SAN007's dual-use/export-control and end-use-obfuscation indicators.

The advisory notes Iran 'often sells its oil below prevailing market prices, offering a significant discount compared to other Gulf states' (p.3) and that Iranian oil is blended with third-country oil or relabeled via forged documents as 'Malaysian blend' to disguise origin (p.4), matching SAN006's price-deviation and goods-misdescription indicators. Treatment is brief relative to the shadow fleet/front company sections, so confidence is medium rather than high.

Page 7 lists structuring of VA transactions into amounts under record-keeping/reporting thresholds as a red flag, directly mirroring cash-structuring/smurfing behaviour. Single bullet, not further developed, hence medium confidence.

Pages 17-18 (printed 17-18) contain a dedicated 'Red Flag Indicators Related to Geographical Risks' section plus a public-domain case study of a VASP repeatedly relocating between jurisdictions with no/weak VA regulation to stay ahead of AML/CFT controls -- the jurisdictional gap is the finding itself, matching SAN008.

Pages 11-13 (printed 9-11) develop an 'Anonymity' section covering mixing/tumbling services, unregistered/unlicensed VASPs, unhosted wallets, and VASPs with weak KYC, illustrated by the AlphaBay and Helix case studies -- matching CMI010's mixer/tumbler, unregistered VASP and high-risk VASP indicators.

Page 8 (Case Study 1) explicitly identifies 'potential use of money mules by professional money launderers', and page 16 (printed 14) devotes a dedicated 'Profile of potential money mule or scam victims' section with Case Study 10, developing the pass-through mule-account pattern across two case studies.

Page 9, Case Study 2 (South Korea) describes stolen funds converted to VA then moved 55 times through 48 separate VASP accounts before reaching a foreign wallet, a classic layering chain; supported by general transaction-pattern bullets but concentrated in a single case study, hence medium confidence.

Pages 12-20 develop, across two full case studies (superyachts, UK residential property), how professional and non-professional enablers use nominee ownership (e.g. 'Associate is the nominee owner of Company X' while 'the DP holds ultimate beneficial ownership and control', p17) and indirect funding chains through multiple UK/offshore companies (p20: 'all three companies are ultimately funded by the DP... reasonable to expect that all three companies are controlled by the DP') to conceal a designated person's continued ownership/control while payments are made through UK banks/NBPSPs.

Pages 20-22 describe enablers 'fronting on behalf of Russian DPs and claim ownership of frozen assets', with a detailed case study of Company L Investments -- a vehicle 'with no presence in the EU but making use of an address' acquired and used by Individual M, assessed as 'a professional enabler fronting for Company Rus and Individual S' to seek control of a UK company's insolvency estate. This matches the front-company mechanism of an entity/person with little genuine substance giving a sanctioned interest a clean face.

Pages 12, 14-15 and 23 describe enablers using cryptoassets as an alternative payment method to provide DPs with liquidity, including 'cryptoasset to fiat transactions (or vice versa) involving a Russian DP's family members or associates' (p15) and a disrupted Russian money laundering network with 'significant exposure to the UK-designated cryptocurrency exchange Garantex' and extensive exploitation of 'dollar-backed stablecoins such as Tether (USDT)' (p23).

Pages 24-27 form a dedicated 'Intermediary Countries' section stating 'just over 25% of suspected breach reports received by OFSI... have made reference to intermediary jurisdictions' and providing a jurisdiction-by-activity breakdown (BVI, Cyprus, Switzerland, UAE, Austria, Turkiye, Cayman Islands) covering ownership/transfer of assets, enabler activity, non-resident banking and crypto transactions -- the jurisdictional footprint itself is presented as the risk signal.

Annex Example 2 (pages 21-23) develops two full worked 'mirror trading' scenarios (via a central platform and off-market) in which associated customers in different jurisdictions place matched offsetting buy/sell orders at pre-agreed prices, ending flat in the security with no genuine change in net position while profit/cash moves between them - the structural definition of wash trading. Para 2.24 (page 10) explicitly states 'Some market-abuse practices (eg wash trading) may also be indicative of money laundering', and the off-market example (page 23) is expressly tied to the Deutsche Bank Final Notice mirror-trading case.

emergent_label: Free of Payment Securities Transfer Laundering
rationale: Annex Example 1 (pages 20-21) describes a customer depositing offshore bonds with Broker 1 (no beneficial-ownership check), then transferring them 'free of payment' to an account at Broker 2 in another jurisdiction without either broker verifying origin/ownership, before the bonds are sold to realise clean cash (page 20: 'Company A has realised clean cash in Country 2'). No Knowledge Centre typology (capital_markets, correspondent_banking or tbml) returned an above-floor match for this free-of-payment custody-transfer mechanism, so it is proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Medium-Term Note / Debt Issuance Layering
rationale: Annex Example 3 (pages 24-25) describes an arranger converting a loan into an MTN via an investment bank that never sees the end investor, with coupon payments routed through an offshore agent to MTN holders who may differ from the initial investor; it later emerges the underlying investor shares controllers/shareholders with the original borrower (page 24: 'a strong link between the borrower and underlying "lender" which could indicate potential embezzlement, money laundering or both'). No Knowledge Centre search for debt-issuance/MTN/offshore-agent structuring returned an above-floor match, so this is proposed as emergent.

Annex Example 4 (pages 25-26) describes an investor with an undisclosed connection to a senior director of the issuer ('This individual has connections with a senior director of the company, though this was not disclosed publicly', page 25) receiving equity worth ten times the value of the convertible loan and selling it for cash - matching PAT009's focus on trading/value transfer between counterparties connected through undisclosed ownership, control or network relationships. Result para (page 26) states funds were washed 'by lending money to the company, which was exchanged for shares that can be sold for more than the value of the loan'.

emergent_label: Omnibus/Reliance Intermediation Opacity
rationale: Annex Example 5 (pages 27-28) describes a UK bank treating an offshore broker's omnibus flow as its customer, applying no EDD and relying on the broker for CDD, only later discovering the broker's underlying customers were high-net-worth, politically-connected individuals with close ties to the broker's directors (page 27: 'the bank has potentially been facilitating the transfer of economic value from one account to another, cross-jurisdiction, without realising that this might have been linked to financial crime'). Knowledge Centre searches for hidden-underlying-customer/omnibus intermediation returned only weak, semantically mismatched results (BA009 Transaction Laundering, a card-rails typology), so this is proposed as emergent.

Annex Example 6 (page 28) describes a customer in a high-risk jurisdiction opening offsetting short-dated FX option positions that generate an initial premium payment into a prime brokerage account at a separate bank, which is then paid straight back on near-immediate expiry with no discernible business rationale. The document states directly: 'The neutralising effect of the trading raises concerns that the intended purpose is to facilitate the layering stage of a money-laundering scheme' (page 28) - matching BA008 Layering's function of pushing funds through a transaction chain to sever the audit trail before integration.

emergent_label: Capital Markets Account Funding Layering
rationale: Annex Example 7 (page 29) gives two brief sub-examples: (a) a corporate customer regularly over-collateralises its prime brokerage account and the excess is returned with 'no questions asked', which 'may appear cleaner as a result'; and (b) a UK broker account receives significant cash, does not trade, then two months later withdraws the cash to a third-party account, which 'seems plausible' was 'entered and withdrawn to make it appear cleaner'. These are brief, undeveloped illustrations (no diagram, hedged language) with no above-floor Knowledge Centre match on account-funding/cash-withdrawal layering, so proposed as emergent at low confidence.

Advisory's core 'Deceptive Shipping Practices' list matches Shadow Fleet indicators: AIS disabling/spoofing (p.2), physical alteration of vessel ID (p.2), ship-to-ship transfers (p.3), false flags and flag hopping (p.3). Annex B corroborates with North Korea coal exports via STS to Chinese barges (p.28), illicit refined-petroleum STS transfers (p.29), and non-AIS-transmitting barges (p.30).

Page 3 'Complex Ownership or Management' section describes bad actors using complex business structures, shell companies and multiple levels of ownership/management to disguise the ultimate beneficial owner of cargo, matching Complex Ownership Structures' layering/opacity indicators. Single dedicated section, hence medium confidence.

Page 3 'Voyage Irregularities' describes disguising origin/destination via indirect routing, unscheduled detours, or transit/transshipment through third countries. Annex B (p.28) documents North Korea coal transshipped via STS transfer to local barges in Chinese territorial waters for onward delivery, matching the Transshipment hub pattern.

Page 2-3 notes sanctions evaders falsifying shipping documentation to disguise the origin of petrochemicals, petroleum and metals; page 15 flags purchases of crude/refined petroleum, petrochemicals and metals at rates significantly below market price as a red flag, matching Trade Based Sanctions Evasion's misdescription and price-deviation indicators. Only brief, scattered mentions, hence low confidence.

emergent_label: Professional Money Laundering (Third-Party PML Organisations/Networks)
rationale: The entire report (pp.8-14, 19) defines and evidences a distinct criminal service category: individuals, PMLOs and PMLNs that launder for a fee/commission for third-party criminal clients (e.g. p.8 'PMLs provide services to criminals and organised crime groups by laundering the proceeds of their illegal activities'; p.12 defines PML as subset of third-party ML paid by commission). No existing KC typology captures this overarching professional-launderer-for-hire business model, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Money Transport and Cash Controller Networks
rationale: Section IV (p.19) describes dedicated international cash-controller/collector/transmitter networks that pool and net cash across jurisdictions, illustrated in detail by Box 2 (p.20-21, controller/collector/transmitter roles, structuring under reporting thresholds) and Box 3 Operation Kandil (p.21-22, EUROPOL-coordinated cash-courier network moving EUR 5m of heroin proceeds). Searches for 'cash courier controller network' returned only partial fits (BA007 Cash Intensive Activity 0.50, PAT010 Hidden Controller 0.45), neither of which captures the specific controller/collector/transmitter cash-transport network structure, so proposed as emergent.

Section IV 'Money Mule Networks' (pp.22-24) describes recruited individuals whose personal bank accounts receive and rapidly forward illicit proceeds on a controller's instruction, matching BA003 Mule Accounts. Box 4 (p.23, Singapore case: funds transferred out or withdrawn within days of receipt) and Box 5 (p.24, Avalanche network mules purchasing goods with stolen funds) both evidence the pass-through mule-account pattern.

emergent_label: Virtual Currency / Digital Money Laundering Networks
rationale: Section IV (p.25-26) and Box 6 (Russian Dark Web drug-store case) describe dedicated networks that move drug-market proceeds through e-wallets, mixers/tumblers and a custom 'transit-panel', then out via debit cards and ATM cash withdrawal by 'cash co-ordinators'. The closest KC search result, CMI010 Cryptocurrency Evasion, is scoped specifically to sanctions evasion via virtual assets, not the generic drug-proceeds layering described here, so the family mismatch means it is not a genuine fit; proposed as emergent.

Section IV 'Proxy Networks' (pp.26-29) sets out a five-step model built entirely on chains of shell companies in multiple jurisdictions used to mix and redistribute client funds (p.26: 'multiple layers of shell companies ... established purely to redistribute and mix funds from various sources'), evidenced by Box 7 (Russian bank-fraud shells), Box 8 (Israeli PMLN shell infrastructure) and Box 9 (Latvia/Cyprus/Estonia shell platform). This matches PAT007 Shell Company Network's indicators of layered ownership, offshore registration and shared control.

Section V 'Trade-Based Money Laundering' (p.30) explicitly lists over/under-invoicing as a PML technique ('Falsifying the number and/or value of goods being shipped to be higher or lower than the corresponding payment ... also known as over or under-invoicing'), developed further in Box 10 Project OROAD (pp.30-31, fraudulent invoices used to account for drug-sale proceeds) and Box 11 (p.32, POS-based currency smuggling with fictitious value transfer).

p.30 lists 'phantom shipments' as a distinct TBML variation used by PMLs: 'The transfer of funds which purport to be related to trade, or to the purchase of goods that are ultimately never shipped or received (also known as "phantom shipments")'. This is a single enumerated bullet without its own dedicated case study, so linked at medium rather than high confidence.

emergent_label: Account Settlement Mechanism (Cross-Border Netting via OCG Accounts)
rationale: Section V 'Account Settlement Mechanisms' (p.33) defines a technique where PMLNs net cash and bank-account balances between OCGs in different countries to avoid cross-border transfers, illustrated by Box 12 (p.33, Belgian construction companies settling drug-trafficking cash for illegal workers) and the account-settlement scenario in Box 2 (p.20-21). Searches returned only generic 'Layering' and 'Complex Ownership' matches with no specific netting/settlement concept, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Underground Banking and Alternative Banking Platforms
rationale: Section V (p.34-35) describes underground banking/hawala and bespoke 'alternative banking platforms' (ABPs) that bypass the regulated financial sector, evidenced by Box 13 (p.34, Canadian underground banking network laundering CAD 1bn/year via IVTS) and Box 14 (p.35, UK ABP moving EUR 400m across four jurisdictions). A dedicated search for 'underground banking hawala alternative banking platform' returned no match above the floor, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Complicit Financial Service Providers and Professional Gatekeepers
rationale: Section VI (pp.35-47) is dedicated to knowing/complicit facilitation of PML by financial-service and DNFBP insiders -- MVTS agents (Box 16-17), bank officers (Box 18-19), lawyers/accountants/TCSPs (Box 20-23), payment processors (Box 24, PacNet) and virtual currency exchangers (Box 25, BTC-e) -- unified by the intro statement (p.35) that PMLs 'occupy positions within the financial services industry ... and DNFBP sectors ... and use their occupation, business infrastructure and knowledge to facilitate ML'. Searches for complicit MVTS/bank/lawyer facilitation returned no qualifying matches, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Money Laundering from Environmental Crime
rationale: The entire report is organised around laundering techniques specific to environmental crime (illegal logging, illegal mining, waste trafficking). No existing library typology captures 'environmental crime' as the underlying predicate/driver. See p.5 ('significant role of trade-based fraud and misuse of shell and front companies to launder gains from illegal logging, illegal mining, and waste trafficking') and p.11 (chapter highlights on specialised networks moving environmental-crime proceeds).

Section 3.2 (p.27) describes criminals using front companies with no genuine legitimate footprint (or comingled with real trade) to move logging/mining/waste proceeds through trade transactions; the Madagascar case (p.28) shows a front-company scheme in the vanilla export trade used to give illicit rosewood proceeds a legitimate commercial face.

Section 3.3 (p.28-29) describes a waste-sector criminal network using overseas shell companies to move funds under invoice cover (Italy case), and p.21-22 describes a South American supply chain relying on a web of domestic shell companies with nominee beneficial owners established by DNFBPs -- both consistent with a shell company network exhibiting layered/nominee ownership.

Section 3.4 (p.29-30) states trade-based fraud for environmental crime 'could include mislabelling of hazardous waste or protected wood to conceal their real value,' and the Italy case (p.31) confirms 'shipping documents were falsified to state that the cargo consisted of goods and raw materials, as opposed to waste.'

Annex A (p.58) describes timber/gold 'exported at below market prices, change ownership and Bill of Lading en route... and is imported at recipient countries at higher declared values,' a classic under-invoicing-at-export pattern; Section 3.4 (p.29-30) confirms the report's focus on under/over-declaration as a common TBML thread for environmental crime.

The cash-intensive nature of mining is highlighted repeatedly (p.14: 'the cash-intensive nature of the industry'), the Madagascar case (p.28) shows bulk cash purchases of vanilla used to co-mingle illicit rosewood proceeds, the Brazil case (p.30) routes funds through hairdressers, and Annex A (p.55) flags 'large cash withdrawals from financial institutions operating in rural areas' near illegal mining/logging as a core detection indicator.

emergent_label: Cyber-Enabled Fraud (CEF) Money Laundering
rationale: The entire 72-page FATF/INTERPOL/Egmont report is built around this technique: pp.5, 15-26 develop CEF-ML networks (BEC, phishing, romance/pig-butchering, investment fraud) run by transnational organised syndicates using mules, shell companies and multi-sector layering; p.63 conclusion restates 'CEF is perpetrated by transnational, organised crime syndicates.' No existing KC typology captures the CEF-ML umbrella itself, though several component techniques (mules, shell networks, TBML, VA laundering) match existing entries and are proposed separately.

Money mule accounts are the report's core first-layer ML mechanism: p.18 para24 defines individual money mules and 'herders'; p.19 Box 8 gives a worked case (83 pass-through transactions); p.62 Box 48 European Money Mule Action identifies 8,755 mules and 222 recruiters. Matches BA003's pass-through/controller-instructed personal account pattern.

Shell company networks used as first-layer/laundering vehicles are extensively documented: p.20 Box 9 (Türkiye) describes 209 companies with mutual accountants incorporated/liquidated on the same dates; p.23 Box 11 (India) describes 36 linked shell entities, 28 with foreign-national directors. Matches PAT007's shared-director/address/short-lived-entity indicators.

p.24 para30 states criminals 'use trade-based money laundering (TBML) techniques such as fictitious or false invoicing' and purchase of high-value goods for resale; p.25 Box 13 (Ireland/Nigeria) shows a Nigerian company paying invoices for legitimate goods with BEC/romance proceeds. This is the closest KC TBML entry to the general invoicing-based technique described, though the report does not specify price inflation specifically, so linked at medium confidence.

p.25 describes VA anonymity-enhancing layering of CEF proceeds: 'unhosted wallets, peer-to-peer transactions, peel chains, and high-risk exchanges... mixers or tumbler services as well as anonymity-enhanced VAs... and decentralised finance (DeFi) services.' Indicator set (mixer/tumbler use, unregistered/high-risk VASP) matches CMI010 even though CMI010's doctrine is authored in a sanctions-evasion context rather than fraud-proceeds laundering; flagged for reviewer in extraction_notes.

emergent_label: Virtual IBAN (vIBAN) Abuse
rationale: Dedicated section 3.2 (pp.28-30) plus Box 18/19: p.31 explains criminals exploit the fact vIBANs are 'optically identical' to real IBANs to reroute victim payments to a rerouted physical master account; p.33 Box 19 (Luxembourg 'Hi Mum' scam) shows six vIBANs used to receive fraud proceeds via a Luxembourg PSP's prepaid card product. No existing KC typology found for vIBAN-specific abuse.

emergent_label: Human Trafficking-Fuelled Scam Centres
rationale: p.15 para19 states victims are 'lured through fake job ads to online call centres and forced to commit CEF on an industrial scale'; p.16 Box 5 (Operation Storm Makers) documents 15 men and one woman trafficked to Cambodia and forced to work as scammers, with 121 arrests across 25 countries. Referenced also in the Executive Summary (p.5). No existing KC typology matches this trafficking-for-fraud-labour pattern.

emergent_label: DPRK Proliferation Financing via Cyber-Enabled Fraud Tools
rationale: p.16 para21 states cybercrime is 'a major source of illicit income generation for the ... DPRK', with proceeds from selling hacking/phishing tools; p.17 Box 6 gives a worked case of DPRK Munitions Industry Department IT workers selling voice-phishing applications later used to defraud ROK victims. No existing KC typology found for this cyber/proliferation-financing nexus.

emergent_label: Underground Banking and HOSSP-Based Professional Money Laundering
rationale: The entire report (pp.5,13-15) is devoted to how underground banking systems and hawala/HOSSPs are misused as informal, decentralised value-transfer infrastructure for professional money laundering, settling obligations via trade, cash pooling, formal channels or asset movement without cross-border movement of funds. No existing Knowledge Centre typology captures this core informal value-transfer/settlement mechanism, so it is proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Digital Hawala / Virtual-Asset-Based Settlement Between Underground Banking Operators
rationale: Subsection 6.5 and 7.1.1 (pp.25-28) plus Boxes 5, 6, 8 and 10 (pp.26-27, 35, 36) describe a distinct, developed technique in which HOSSPs settle inter-operator balances using stablecoins/VAs (fiat-to-VA-to-fiat conversion, wallet-to-wallet transfer), sometimes combined with gold, as a cross-cutting settlement enabler. No crypto-family typology exists in the Knowledge Centre, so this is proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Underground Banking / HOSSP Nexus with Terrorist Financing
rationale: Subsection 7.1.4 (pp.32-34) is a dedicated section, corroborated by a concrete Turkish case (Box 8, p.35) involving cash seizures and hawala records linked to ISIL financing, establishing HOSSPs as connective TF infrastructure. No terrorist_financing family typology currently exists in the Knowledge Centre, so this is proposed as emergent.

Page 23 (para 71ii) states that trade-based settlement in underground banking/HOSSP schemes includes 'over- and under-invoicing, falsified or manipulated shipping documents, invoice manipulation, and phantom shipments' used by import/export front companies to balance inter-operator accounts, matching TBML001 Over Invoicing.

Page 23 (para 71ii) and the India case study on page 24 ('Trading entities imported genuine goods at deliberately understated values, leaving an undisclosed balance payable abroad') describe under-invoicing used to settle underground banking obligations, matching TBML002U Under Invoicing.

Page 22 (para 70) describes 'clearing via third-party transfers... settlement of balances through unconnected third parties' where debts are cleared via invoices or commercial obligations paid by parties other than the trade counterparty, matching TBML008 Third Party Payment Abuse.

The India case study (p.24, Box 3) describes shell companies 'incorporated through nominees, often using stolen or forged KYC documents, and had limited or no genuine business activity' used with circular trade flows to move value, matching TBML009 Shell Company Trading.

emergent_label: Black Market Peso Exchange (BMPE) Trade-Based Settlement
rationale: Subsection 7.2.3 (pp.36-38) is dedicated to BMPE as a Latin American trade- and currency-based ML mechanism mirroring underground banking, illustrated by Box 11 (p.38-39, Operation Cymbal) exploiting Venezuela's controlled exchange rate via false invoices and parallel-market cash sales. No BMPE-specific typology was returned by search, so this is proposed as emergent within the tbml family.

Page 24 (para 74) states 'Third party money mules are commonly used to fragment large-sum criminal cash into multiple small deposits and transfer them to designated accounts, avoiding the AML monitoring thresholds of FIs', and mule accounts recur in Box 5 (Turkiye, p.26), Box 12 (Spain, p.41) and Box 29 (India, p.68), matching BA003 Mule Accounts.

emergent_label: High-Capacity Transnational PML Networks / International Controller Networks (ICN)
rationale: Page 21 defines 'controllers'/'international controller networks (ICNs)' as trusted individuals co-ordinating collectors, transmitters and correspondent brokers across jurisdictions. Subsection 7.2.4 (pp.40-42), corroborated by Box 12 (Spain, Operation Karasu, p.41-42, documenting 32 transactions worth over EUR 5.5 million and a wallet processing over USD 21 million), describes scalable, commercially organised cross-border PML service networks (including so-called 'Chinese-speaking money laundering networks'). This organisational/controller-network typology is broader than PAT010 Hidden Controller (which addresses concealed beneficial control of a single entity) and is proposed as emergent within the network family.

Page 12 table defines Over Invoicing: seller misrepresents price above true value to gain excess value from the buyer's payment, as one of the transfer-of-value methods the paper describes for Trade Finance FCR.
Page 12 table defines Under Invoicing: buyer gains excess value where the invoice understates the true price, listed alongside over-invoicing as a core transfer-of-value method.
Page 12 table describes Multiple Invoicing: issuing more than one invoice for the same goods to justify multiple payments, harder to detect when more than one FI is used.
Page 12 table describes Phantom Shipping: no goods are shipped and all supporting documentation is completely falsified.

Page 12 table covers Short Shipping, Over Shipping and Deliberate Obfuscation of Type of Goods -- misrepresenting quantity, quality or type of goods in documentation to disguise true value, matching False Description of Goods doctrine.

Dual use goods are developed across multiple sections: definition and NPWMD framing at page 14, the Challenges discussion of civil/military application items at page 16, and the Limitations discussion at page 21 on why FI trade staff cannot reliably identify dual-use goods, showing the paper develops rather than merely mentions the technique.
Page 14 mentions trade based sanctions as embargoes on provision of certain goods, services or expertise to certain countries, a single passing reference rather than a developed scenario.

Glossary entry on TBML at pages 30-31 specifically describes Funnel Accounts as part of a TBML typology, noting funds moved against false invoices into the trade relationship account, and that the trading company may have been taken over by money launderers to facilitate layering.

Dedicated 'Sanctions evasion' section (pp.77-78) describes a case where military-grade goods were exported to Russia in violation of EU sanctions via front companies and falsified documentation, and states trade-based sanctions evasion relies on a crime-as-a-service model with infiltration of legitimate trade supply chains.

p.77 case example states illicit military exports to Russia were 'facilitated through front companies and falsified documentation'; p.78 states 'front companies are set up in retail, import-export, transport, or the financial sector for the procurement and shipment of goods or assets' to maintain beneficial ownership by sanctioned actors.

p.77 forward-looking statement that criminal networks 'increasingly leverage tools such as ... anonymised financial transactions, cryptocurrencies and blockchain technologies, and cyber-enabled trade-based money laundering' to evade sanctions; single mention, not a developed case, hence low confidence.

p.27 notes 'front or shell companies may be used to facilitate the movement of illicit or stolen goods or to enable money laundering activities'; p.75 customs fraudsters 'make use of limited liability companies, individual entrepreneurs, and shell companies, which they quickly establish and dissolve'; p.75 VAT/MTIC section: 'Shell or buffer companies, whether infiltrated or set-up, facilitate the exploitation of cross-border VAT systems and VAT refund processes.'

emergent_label: Cryptocurrency Layering via Mixing Services, Chain-Hopping and DeFi
rationale: p.25 dedicated case example (ChipMixer) describes deposited funds turned into 'chips' then mixed to anonymise trails, alongside narrative on 'chain hopping' between cryptocurrencies, crypto-swapping services, privacy coins (Monero) and DeFi protocols used to obscure the origin of illicit funds; no existing KC crypto-family typology captures this general (non-sanctions) crypto layering technique, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Corruption Brokers and Digitalised Corruption-as-a-Service
rationale: Dedicated 'Corruption' section (pp.28-29) describes corruption 'adapting ... to the crime-as-a-service model with the emergence of corruption brokers' (p.23), online recruitment of corrupt insiders with access to digital systems, and bribes 'transferred by criminally exploiting cryptocurrencies or fintech' (p.29). No corruption-family typology exists yet in the KC, so proposed as emergent.

emergent_label: Hybrid Threat Actor Use of Criminal Networks as Proxies (Woodpecker Modus Operandi)
rationale: This is a central, extensively developed thesis of the report (pp.11, 14-15): criminal networks increasingly act as proxies for state/hybrid threat actors, conducting sabotage, cyber-attacks, disinformation and money laundering for geopolitical as well as financial ends, described via the 'woodpecker' pattern of persistent, cumulative, low-level destabilising incidents rather than a single attack. No existing family/typology in the KC library captures this state-criminal nexus pattern.

The entire report (106 case studies analysed) is organised around tracing effective ownership/control chains back to the natural person, exactly FND003's function. See p.7 ('Analysis of 106 case studies demonstrates that legal persons, principally shell companies, are a key feature...') and Annex D pp.174-179 which catalogues techniques (IP address analysis, shareholder registers, MLA, etc.) used to compute who ultimately owns/controls an entity.

Section 2 'Generating complex ownership and control structures' (pp.25-27) is a fully developed technique: 'Adding numerous layers of ownership between an asset and the beneficial owner in different jurisdictions...can prevent detection and frustrate investigations' (p.28), illustrated by Case Study 88 (Russia) showing a multi-jurisdiction ownership chain (Delaware->BVI->US->France).

Shell/shelf/front companies are identified as the dominant vehicle across the case sample: 'shell companies are the most common type of legal person used in schemes...to obscure beneficial ownership' (p.31), with dedicated indicator sub-list 'Indicators of shell companies' (Annex E, p.186) covering shared addresses, no personnel, no physical presence -- matching PAT007's exact indicator set.

Formal and informal nominee directors/shareholders who exercise no real control but conceal the true controller are developed at length pp.36-41 ('A nominee shareholder is the registered owner of shares held for the benefit of another person', p.38), with multiple case studies (77, 80, 81, 87) of straw men/hidden controllers.

The 'loan-back'/'round-robin' technique described p.45 ('money being sent to companies which are owned or controlled by...the same individual, and returned in the guise of a loan') and Case Studies 5 and 8 describe funds looping back to the originating beneficial owner, matching Circular Ownership; supported by fewer case studies than the layered-ownership/shell-company themes, hence medium confidence.

emergent_label: Professional Intermediary (TCSP/Legal/Accounting) Gatekeeper Complicity in Beneficial Ownership Concealment
rationale: Section 3 (pp.46-85) is a dedicated, fully developed technique with its own 'continuum of complicity' model (p.50, Figure 1) running from innocent involvement to complicit, and 10 named vulnerabilities (establishing legal persons, shelf companies, directorship/virtual office, trust accounts, real estate, tax advice, LPP, limited AML/CFT obligations). No existing Knowledge Centre typology captures gatekeeper-complicity as a technique in its own right (searches for 'professional intermediaries lawyers accountants gatekeepers' returned no match above floor), so this is proposed as emergent.

Advisory (p.3) extensively describes the 2RIVERS network's use of 'over 100 Shadow Fleet oil tankers, vessels which are usually over 15 years old' employing 'switching off the ship's automatic identification system (AIS)', 'ship-to-ship transfers to obscure the origin of the oil' and 'regularly changing flags' -- matching SAN002 indicators directly. SAN002 is TWIN of PAT008 (network family); this advisory is issued by NCA/OFSI/FCDO explicitly to address sanctions evasion in Russian oil sales (p.2), so the sanctions-family twin SAN002 is the correct fit per the stated convention.

P.3 describes the 'red' side of the network as having 'deliberately obscure ownership structures and many front companies designed to be replaced with ease if they are subject to Western sanctions.' P.5 red-flag list adds 'Limited information on ownership, directors or beneficiaries' and 'limited online presence with no company website... generic stock photos, and no details on the individuals operating the company' -- directly matching SAN004 indicators (no employees/premises, no web presence, generic description, opaque ownership).

Worked example on p.4: oil purchased from ROSNEFT by a 'red' company in a high-risk jurisdiction is moved on a Shadow Fleet vessel 'to a terminal in a third-party location', refined and 'sold' to a 'blue' network company which sells to an end customer with 'no sight of its Russian origins.' P.3 also references 'transhipments of oil and mixing operations to hide the Russian origin.' This matches SAN003's core mechanic of routing through an intermediary hub to disguise true origin and defeat origin-based sanctions controls.

Advisory is framed as a sanctions Red Alert (NCA/OFSI/FCDO) and describes a fleet of over 100 shadow fleet tankers (p.3) using AIS switching, ship-to-ship transfers and flag changes to carry Russian oil, with 400+ vessels now sanctioned. Sanctions framing means the sanctions twin SAN002 is preferred over PAT008 per doctrine convention.

The 'red' side of the network is described as having 'many front companies designed to be replaced with ease if they are subject to Western sanctions' (p.3), and red flag indicators list companies with limited online presence, generic stock photos and no contact information (p.5), matching the Front Companies doctrine.

The network's 'red' side is described as having 'deliberately obscure ownership structures' (p.3) and the red flag indicators include 'limited information on ownership, directors or beneficiaries' (p.5), matching the Ownership Evasion doctrine's concealment of beneficial control.

The worked example (p.4) describes oil purchased from ROSNEFT being moved on a shadow fleet vessel to a terminal in a third-party location where it is 'sold' to another network company before onward sale, obscuring true origin -- a classic transshipment-hub pattern, reinforced by p.3's reference to 'transhipments of oil and mixing operations to hide the Russian origin.'

Advisory is framed as sanctions evasion (NCA/OFSI Red Alert on Russian oil sanctions). Page 3 describes '2RIVERS network utilises over 100 Shadow Fleet oil tankers... use deceptive shipping practices' including switching off AIS, ship-to-ship transfers and regularly changing flags, with over 400 Shadow Fleet vessels sanctioned. This matches SAN002 Shadow Fleet rather than its network-family twin PAT008, per the convention that sanctions-framed advisories take the sanctions twin.

Page 3 states the 'red' side has 'deliberately obscure ownership structures and many front companies designed to be replaced with ease if they are subject to Western sanctions'; page 4 confirms the network will keep 'replacing sanctioned entities with freshly incorporated companies clean of sanctions but fulfilling the same role'. Page 5 red flags (limited ownership/director info, no genuine web presence/generic stock photos, limited trading history) mirror SAN004's front-company indicator set.

Page 3 states 'Money and oil move between the companies through transhipments of oil and mixing operations to hide the Russian origin.' The page 4 worked example describes oil moving via a Shadow Fleet vessel to 'a terminal in a third-party location' before being sold on to a second network company and then the ultimate customer, matching SAN003's routing-through-an-intermediary-hub technique. Only two passages develop this specific mechanic, so confidence is medium rather than high.

Red flag 9 on page 4 states the customer's name or address is similar to a party on the OFSI consolidated list - this is exactly the name-form evasion of list screening (near-match/variant names that defeat exact-match filters) that SAN005 defines, and is not covered by the already-claimed front-company or transshipment typologies.

Red flags 1 and 12 on page 4 flag companies based in, or using open accounts/lines of credit in conjunction with, 'known diversionary destinations' - the entity's own jurisdictional footprint (registration/operating location, trade corridor) is itself the risk signal, matching SAN008's mechanism, distinct from the already-claimed SAN003 Transshipment (physical routing through intermediate points) and SAN004 Front Companies (corporate substance).

SAN006 has cross-family twin TBML010 (Sanctions Evasion Through Trade); SAN006 is preferred because this is a UK NCA/OFSI Red Alert explicitly framed as sanctions/export-control evasion on Russia-bound high-risk goods. Red flag 4 on page 4 (customer significantly overpays for a Common High Priority list item versus known market prices) matches SAN006's mechanism of manipulating the trade transaction itself via invoice mispricing/large price deviation from benchmark, distinct from the already-claimed dual-use, transshipment and front-company typologies.

Page 8 red flag: government contracts 'consistently awarded, through an opaque selection process, to the same legal entity or entities that share similar beneficial ownership structures.' This is the PAT002 mechanism -- entities connected through a common beneficial owner/ultimate controller -- applied to public procurement: the same hidden UBO sits behind multiple 'competing' bidders, letting a kleptocrat's network capture government contracts while appearing to be independent counterparties.

Page 6: 'Corrupt actors may also leverage their family members and close associates to create shell companies and open business or personal accounts on their behalf while retaining control of the accounts.' Page 9 red flag: 'Assets held in the name of intermediate legal entities whose beneficial owner or owners are tied to a kleptocrat or his or her family member.' This matches PAT010's mechanism of an individual exercising effective control over an entity despite not appearing as the declared owner -- the kleptocrat is the hidden controller behind nominee family/associate ownership.

Indicators 11, 28, 29 and 32 (pages 10-12) flag holding companies and payment counterparties purely by their jurisdictional footprint - offshore/former-Soviet registration, Swiss/BVI/Cypriot legal persons, and Fintech/PSP transactions routed to or from Russia, Belarus, FATF-deficient or comprehensively sanctioned jurisdictions - with no further ownership or trade element required for the flag to fire. This is SAN008's own mechanism: jurisdiction footprint IS the finding, not an aggravating detail of another finding.

Indicators 20-21 (page 11) describe off-the-shelf corporations with no trading record and nominee ownership, incorporated by the same people at a shared registered office, used as 'throughputs' to move shares from sanctioned to non-sanctioned entities - matching SAN004's mechanism of a substance-less entity that exists purely to transact while the real (sanctioned) party stays hidden behind it.

Indicator 34 (page 12) explicitly names circumvention via 'Open Account Trade-Based Money Laundering' through 'increases in third party open account payments' - the trade is settled by a payer who is not the counterparty, which is TBML008's defining mechanism of breaking the link between the trade and the funds.

emergent_label: Citizenship-by-Investment Nationality Laundering
rationale: Indicators 12-13 (pages 10-11) describe DPs/UBOs changing nationality via golden-passport/citizenship-by-investment or investor-visa schemes so that ownership records show a non-Russian third-country nationality rather than a layering/nominee structure. No existing typology (searched: citizenship by investment, golden passport, name screening evasion) captures nationality substitution via CBI programmes as the evasion mechanism itself, distinct from ownership-chain layering (SAN001) or name-spelling screening evasion (SAN005).

emergent_label: Enabler Pooled Account Screening Concealment
rationale: Indicator 18 (page 11) describes pooled accounts where 'banks see only the name of the enabler and not the client', used to move funds to DP-linked entities. This conceals the true customer from the bank's own screening via the account structure itself, distinct from funnel accounts (BA002, which is about deposit volume/dispersion) or card-rail transaction laundering (BA009). Single-bullet evidence, no matching doctrine found on search, so confidence is low.

Case Study 99 (p.31-32/45-46) describes front companies (the Alavi Foundation's 60% stake in a Manhattan office tower) used to hold and channel US assets on behalf of Bank Melli, an entity designated by US authorities for financing Iran's nuclear/ballistic missile program under UNSCR 1803 -- the front company gave the designated party's interest a clean commercial face while funds were transferred back to Bank Melli. Case Study 105 similarly describes OFAC designating shell/front companies tied to a straw man used to hold real estate on behalf of a Kingpin Act-designated PEP. Both match SAN004's mechanism of an entity with no genuine economic substance holding accounts/assets while the real, designated party stays hidden behind it.

Paragraphs 96-99 describe a 'loan-back'/'round-robin' technique in detail: funds are paid out via false invoices to an entity controlled by the same beneficial owner, pool there, then return to the original owner (or a relative) disguised as a private loan. Case Study 5 is explicitly titled the 'Round Robin' scheme and states funds 'ultimately returned to the original beneficiary'; Case Studies 6, 7 and 8 (pp.45-46, 114-116) show the same pattern through international bank accounts in Hong Kong, Samoa and secrecy jurisdictions, with funds cleared hop-to-hop with negligible loss and returned to the origin under the guise of unrelated loan/consultancy activity. This matches BA004's definition of a round-tripping loop where funds leave an origin, pass through intermediary accounts, and return to the same control having taken on the appearance of unrelated third-party activity.

emergent_label: Bearer Share Anonymous Ownership Transfer
rationale: Paragraphs 81-83 (p.36) devote a dedicated subsection to bearer shares/bearer share warrants as a distinct BO-concealment instrument: ownership is 'legally owned by the person that has physical possession of the bearer share certificate,' exchanged 'anonymously between parties by way of physical exchange alone, as no record of the exchange needs to be documented or reported.' FATF Recommendation 24 specifically requires measures against their misuse. Case Study 12 (Canada, p.118) and Case Study 92 (Switzerland, p.162) both involve the off-market transfer of bearer shares to anonymise control of shell entities used in securities fraud and stolen-asset concealment schemes. This is a mechanically distinct concealment technique from the layered/circular ownership chains already captured (no registry entry or transfer record exists at all, versus a traceable but obscured chain), so it merits its own typology rather than folding into existing ownership-layering patterns.

emergent_label: Beneficiary Flooding to Obscure Transaction Attribution
rationale: Paragraph 93 (p.41-42) describes 'Declaring Numerous Beneficiaries' as a technique where 'large numbers of customers have been declared as beneficiaries on a single bank account in such a way that the bank has difficulty establishing which transaction was made on behalf of which beneficiary,' obscuring the ultimate beneficial owner rather than the ownership structure itself. Case Study 38 (Israel, p.44) evidences this directly: 'More than 60 beneficiaries were declared to the bank as beneficiaries, in such a way that the bank had difficulty in establishing which transaction was made on behalf of which beneficiary.' This is a transaction-attribution obfuscation technique distinct from the corporate-structure and nominee techniques already captured, since it operates entirely within a single account's beneficiary declarations rather than through layered entities or controllers.

Red flag 4 (page 4) states a customer 'significantly overpays for a Common High Priority list item, compared to known market prices.' This is the classic over-invoicing mechanism -- price inflated beyond true market value to move excess value cross-border, here used to disguise/fund sanctioned procurement.

Red flag 9 (page 4) flags customers whose 'name or its address is similar to one of the parties on the OFSI consolidated list' -- i.e. a near-match name engineered to slip past exact-match list screening, which is precisely SAN005's mechanism of defeating screening through the form of the name.

Red flag 11 (page 4) flags 'companies that are physically co-located, or have shared ownership, with an entity on the OFSI consolidated list.' This is PAT002's mechanism of entities connected through a common beneficial owner/controller, matching its own indicator 'Ownership connected to sanctioned entity'.

Page 4-5 TLI/TENEX bribery case: Lambert and co-conspirators 'caused fake invoices to be prepared, purportedly from TENEX to TLI, which described services that were never provided,' then wired the corrupt payments to shell companies in Latvia, Cyprus, and Switzerland. This is a paper-only trade (invoice + payment, no genuine service delivered) used to justify a cross-border payment, matching TBML004's Phantom Shipping mechanism exactly, not merely sharing vocabulary.

Red flag on page 8-9: government-contract invoices 'that include charges at substantially higher prices than market rates.' This directly matches TBML001's mechanism of price inflation beyond true market value, applied here to government procurement invoices used to move corruption proceeds.

Page 6: 'Corrupt actors may also leverage their family members and close associates to create shell companies and open business or personal accounts on their behalf while retaining control of the accounts.' Page 9 red flag: 'Assets held in the name of intermediate legal entities whose beneficial owner or owners are tied to a kleptocrat or his or her family member.' Both describe the kleptocrat exercising effective control over accounts/entities while a nominee (family member/associate) is the declared owner -- matching PAT010's 'control without ownership' / concealed ownership arrangement mechanism, distinct from PAT007's network-structure detection already claimed.

Indicator 34 (page 12) flags 'Circumvention attempts through Open Account Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) typology, such as increases in third party open account payments.' TBML008 Third Party Payment Abuse's mechanism is a trade 'settled through a payer who is not the trade counterparty,' breaking the link between the trade and the funds so the true source/destination is obscured. This indicator names exactly that sub-technique (third-party payer on open account trade) as a distinct sanctions-circumvention vector separate from TBML010's sanctioned-party/jurisdiction trade mechanism already claimed for this advisory. Single-bullet evidence supports medium rather than high confidence.

Page 3: a DP who 'claim[s] to have relinquished the asset' will 'retain their influence through trusted proxies and enablers.' Indicator 26 (page 11): a nominee director manages assets with ownership 'obscured through... nominee shareholders and a deed of trust,' DP 'claiming to have divested.' Matches PAT010's mechanism -- control exercised 'despite not appearing as the declared owner, director or controller' -- its 'Control Without Ownership'/'Nominee director structure' indicators. Distinct from SAN001: ownership has genuinely passed to a third party here; the finding is behavioural control retained after real divestment, not an unresolved ownership chain reaching the DP.

Paras 97-99 (p.45-46) describe a 'loan-back'/'round-robin' scheme where funds are sent to a commonly-controlled company and returned as a disguised loan. Case Study 6 (p.46) shows funds returned to the originator 'less the accountant's 10% fee' - matching BA004's round-trip-with-negligible-erosion mechanism exactly. Case Studies 5, 7, 8 develop the same pattern across multiple jurisdictions.

Para 71 (p.33) states informal nominees are solicited 'to establish front companies as a means of circumventing due diligence, money laundering controls or sanctions.' Case Study 99 (p.34) is a concrete sanctions-evasion instance: front companies concealed ownership of US real estate by Bank Melli, an entity designated for supporting Iran's nuclear/ballistic programs and subject to UNSCR 1803 enhanced vigilance, resulting in DOJ forfeiture.

Annex D, para 39 (p.181) dedicates a technique to this exact pattern: 'Search existing records for the same addresses or telephone numbers... large numbers of shell companies... will be registered to the same address.' Case Study 77 (p.42) confirms the mechanism in practice: 'The address listed on the companies' register was the same virtual office in Auckland as the TCSP,' shared across hundreds of companies. This is the shared-address linkage pattern, distinct from the ownership-chain typologies already claimed.

Annex D para 37 (p.179) sets out this exact detection technique: 'By analysing the directors and senior management of a company, it may be possible to discern whether one of them is the ultimate beneficial owner.' The Annex E indicator 'Director, controlling shareholder(s) and/or beneficial owner(s) are listed against the accounts of other legal persons or arrangements' recurs across multiple case studies (e.g. Case Study 30, Guernsey), evidencing the shared-director linkage pattern distinct from the already-claimed hidden-controller conclusion typology.

Para 206 explicitly frames this as TBML: 'legal persons can facilitate trade-based money laundering (TBML) typologies... The Israeli case study (Case Study 40) demonstrates how companies... were used to facilitate TBML through false invoicing.' Case Study 40 (p.81) shows Company A (foreign shell, related-party trading with Company B) transferring real trading revenue to the local company C under cover of a 'consulted fee/service commission... less than half of the real income' - the true trade value is deflated on the visible record, matching Under Invoicing's mechanism of understating value to move it outside the visible trade and evade obligations.

emergent_label: Bearer Share / Bearer Instrument Anonymised Transfer
rationale: Paras 81-83 (p.38) dedicate a distinct subsection to bearer shares as a beneficial-ownership concealment mechanism: 'Ownership and control of bearer shares can be exchanged anonymously between parties by way of physical exchange alone, as no record of the exchange needs to be documented or reported,' making determination of beneficial ownership 'nearly impossible.' This is tied to a specific FATF Recommendation 24 obligation and evidenced in Case Study 12 (Canada). No existing typology in the library (network, sanctions, tbml, or fraud families) captures this specific instrument-based anonymisation mechanism, distinct from nominee/shell-company concealment.

Red flag 9 (page 4) flags a customer whose name or address is similar to one of the parties on the OFSI consolidated list. SAN005 doctrine defines Name Screening Evasion as defeat of list-based screening via near-matches/variants of a listed name that an exact filter would not catch. The red flag's 'similar to' language describes exactly this fuzzy-match screening-evasion scenario rather than an exact hit.

Red flag 13 (page 5) describes a last-minute change in payment routing previously scheduled from a country of concern, now routed through a different country or company. TBML008 doctrine defines Third Party Payment Abuse as settlement through a payer/route that does not match the original trade, breaking the link between trade and funds to obscure true source. The rerouting through a different company/country at the last minute matches this payment-mismatch mechanism, though the advisory develops it in only one bullet.

SAN006 is twin of TBML010 (Sanctions Evasion Through Trade); SAN006 is preferred here because this advisory is explicitly framed as sanctions/export-control circumvention (Russia high-priority goods evasion, issued by NECC/OFSI/FCDO). Red flag 4 (page 4) describes a customer significantly overpaying for a Common High Priority list item versus known market prices. SAN006 doctrine defines Trade-Based Sanctions Evasion as moving value or prohibited goods across a sanctioned boundary by manipulating the trade transaction, e.g. mispricing an invoice, with 'large price deviation from benchmark (over/under-pricing)' as a listed indicator -- this is exactly what red flag 4 evidences.

Red flag on page 8 flags government contracts 'consistently awarded, through an opaque selection process, to the same legal entity or entities that share similar beneficial ownership structures,' and page 9 flags 'assets held in the name of intermediate legal entities whose beneficial owner or owners are tied to a kleptocrat or his or her family member.' Both describe two or more entities connected through a common UBO, matching PAT002's intelligence question directly, distinct from the broader shell-company-network characterization already claimed under PAT007.

Page 5 case study details fake invoices from TENEX to TLI describing services 'never provided,' used solely to justify wiring corrupt payments to shell companies in Latvia, Cyprus and Switzerland -- a paper trade with no genuine underlying delivery used to justify a cross-border payment, matching TBML004 Phantom Shipping's mechanism (payment/invoice with no genuine movement behind it). Page 9 red flag on fictitious invoices for international transactions reinforces the pattern.

Page 9 red flag describes government contract invoices carrying 'charges at substantially higher prices than market rates,' matching TBML001's core mechanism of intentional price inflation beyond true market value used to move illicit value through contract/trade documentation. Single bullet, domestic-contract domain rather than cross-border goods trade, hence low confidence.

Indicator 21 (p.11) describes 'a large number of off-the-shelf corporations with no trading record with nominee ownership used as throughputs.' SAN004 Front Companies doctrine defines the technique as an entity with little/no genuine economic substance established to give a sanctioned interest a clean commercial face, existing purely to transact while the real party stays hidden -- matching the off-the-shelf/no-trading-record/nominee-ownership/throughput description exactly. Distinct from the already-claimed SAN009 (opacity of the ownership chain) and PAT007 (network clustering via shared directors/addresses), which the extraction already covers -- this indicator is about the sham transactional entity itself.

Indicator 34 (p.12) states: 'Circumvention attempts through Open Account Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) typology, such as increases in third party open account payments.' TBML008 Third Party Payment Abuse doctrine defines the mechanism as a trade settled by a payer who is not the trade counterparty, breaking the link between the trade and the funds. The advisory explicitly names 'third party' payments under open-account trade as the sanctions-circumvention mechanism, matching TBML008's core mechanism, distinct from the already-claimed TBML010/SAN006 (sanctioned party or jurisdiction directly party to the trade).

Paras 96-99 (p.45) develop a loan-back/round-robin scheme as a distinct method: funds are paid via invoices to a company controlled by the same beneficial owner and returned disguised as a loan, closing the loop with no genuine economic purpose. Case Study 5 (p.70, explicitly titled the Round Robin scheme), Case Study 6, 7, 8 and 88 all show value cycling back to the originator through a chain of related entities. This matches TBML006's mechanism of value leaving and returning to the same origin through a closed loop of related parties, which is not covered by the already-claimed ownership/network typologies.

Case Study 99 (p.33) describes front companies used to conceal ownership of US assets by Bank Melli, an entity previously designated by US authorities for supporting Iran's nuclear/ballistic missile program and subject to UNSCR 1803 enhanced vigilance -- squarely matching SAN004's mechanism of a front company giving a sanctioned interest a clean commercial face while the real designated party stays hidden. Para 71 (p.32) further ties front-company use directly to circumventing money laundering controls or sanctions. This sanctions-specific mechanism is distinct from the already-claimed ownership-concealment typologies, which do not address designated-party concealment.

Para 206 (p.79) explicitly states legal persons facilitate trade-based money laundering (TBML) typologies, including those that do not result in the actual movement of goods. Case Study 40 (p.81) evidences this directly: a TCSP registers two international shell companies that traded with each other exclusively and did not have any other source of income to disguise the true source and ownership of trading revenue for tax evasion. This matches TBML009's mechanism of routing trade through a shell counterparty with no genuine commercial substance to give illicit trade a legitimate face -- a trade-transaction-specific technique distinct from the already-claimed network/ownership shell-company typology.

Page 5 red-flag list (Grinin Indictment allegations) states defendants were 'Using aliases for the identities of the intermediaries and end users' to run the Russia procurement scheme. SAN005 Name Screening Evasion doctrine defines the mechanism as defeating list-based screening through the form of the name -- aliases that let a party transact under a name a screening filter never flags. The intermediaries/end users here are exactly the parties whose true (potentially listed) identity a bank or exporter's screening would need to catch; aliasing them is the doctrine's mechanism.

Page 2 red-flag list states: 'Payment coming from a third-party country or business not listed on the End-User Statement or other applicable end-user form.' TBML008 Third Party Payment Abuse doctrine defines the mechanism as a trade settled by a payer who is not the trade counterparty, breaking the link between the trade and the funds. This red flag names that exact pattern: settlement funds arriving from a party/country absent from the underlying end-user paperwork.

Page 5 (Grinin Indictment allegations) states defendants were 'Transferring funds from shell companies in foreign jurisdictions into U.S. bank accounts and quickly forwarding or distributing funds to obfuscate the audit trail.' BA005 Rapid Movement doctrine defines its mechanism specifically by velocity -- funds clearing back out almost immediately -- distinct from BA008 Layering's distance/opacity axis (already claimed). The 'quickly forwarding' language matches the velocity mechanism BA005 names, not merely the multi-hop distance BA008 covers. Single-sentence evidence supports low confidence only.

emergent_label: Shipment Splitting to Evade Export Control Detection
rationale: Page 5 (Grinin Indictment allegations) states defendants were 'Dividing shipments of controlled items into multiple, smaller shipments to try to avoid law enforcement detection.' No existing typology covers splitting a physical shipment of goods into smaller consignments to stay under detection/enforcement radar: BA001 Structuring addresses cash deposits under a CTR threshold (financial, not physical goods), and TBML003 Multiple Invoicing addresses invoicing a single shipment multiple times, not dividing a shipment into multiple physical movements. This is a distinct export-control evasion technique the library does not yet capture.

Doc (p3) states the network is 'run by' sanctioned individuals EYYUB and GARAYEV whose personal relationship with ROSNEFT's CEO gives privileged access, and the 'red' side has 'deliberately obscure ownership structures and many front companies designed to be replaced with ease if they are subject to Western sanctions.' P4 confirms 'the people behind it will likely continue to attempt to manipulate the system... by replacing sanctioned entities with freshly incorporated companies... fulfilling the same role.' This matches PAT010 Hidden Controller's mechanism of individuals exercising effective control over a network despite not appearing as declared owner/director, evidenced here by control persisting across serially rotated front entities and indirect sanctions exposure of the personally-sanctioned controllers.

Page 7 states registered import/export values show 'significant mismatches' to foreign bank transfer volumes, and that trade/customs documents 'are missing, appear to be counterfeits, include false or misleading information'. This is the phantom-shipping pattern: a payment and paperwork trail exist but the underlying goods movement does not match or cannot be evidenced (missing shipment / document discrepancy / payment without delivery), matching TBML004's doctrine indicators directly.

Page 5 flags 'unexplained periods of dormancy'; page 6 flags a 'newly formed or recently re-activated trade entity' suddenly engaging in 'high-volume and high-value trade activity'; page 8 flags transaction volume that 'increases in volume quickly and significantly, and then goes dormant after a short period'. Together these describe the idle-then-surge lifecycle contrast that is BA006's defining signal.

Page 5: 'Owners or senior managers of a trade entity appear to be nominees acting to conceal the actual beneficial owners, e.g. they lack experience in business management or lack knowledge of transaction details, or they manage multiple companies.' This is a direct description of PAT010's 'Nominee director structure' / 'Concealed ownership arrangement' / 'Control without ownership' indicators.

Page 5 flags registration at 'a mass registration address, e.g. high-density residential buildings, post-box addresses, commercial buildings or industrial complexes' and its footnote clarifies this 'may also include the address of a trust and company service provider that manages a number of shell companies on behalf of its customers' -- i.e. multiple entities sharing one address, matching PAT005's 'entities connected through a shared address' / 'Address linked to shell companies' indicator.

Page 8: 'Incoming wire transfers to a trade-related account are split and forwarded to non-related multiple accounts that have little or no connection to commercial activity', alongside cash deposits 'transferred to persons or entities in free trade zones or offshore jurisdictions without a business relationship to the account holder'. This matches BA008's mechanism of splitting a seed amount into fragments moved through unrelated intermediaries and offshore jurisdictions to sever the audit trail, distinct from the circular (BA004) or same-day pass-through (BA005) patterns already captured.

Page 7 describes CMLNs using shell or front companies to resell/export purchased U.S. goods. Page 10 red flags describe businesses owned by Chinese nationals receiving marketplace deposits but never purchasing inventory (no commercial footprint), and Hong Kong registered trading companies 'with shell-like characteristics' sending funds with no apparent business or economic purpose -- directly matching TBML009's Shell Counterparty / No Commercial Footprint indicators.

Page 10 red flag: a U.S.-based escrow company receives real estate purchase funds from an unaffiliated, foreign-based shell company in a disparate line of business -- an unrelated third-party payer breaking the link between the real estate transaction and the funds' true origin. Page 6 similarly describes CMLNs purchasing cashier's checks payable to a beneficially-owned shell company, matching TBML008's third-party-payer/shell-structure mechanism.

Page 6 describes CMLN money mules engaging in 'smurfing' operations across multiple depository institution branches to deposit illicit funds into money mule accounts, which are then rapidly moved via wire, ACH, or P2P transfers to separate beneficiary accounts -- matching BA002's collection pattern of geographically dispersed deposits funnelled onward to downstream beneficiaries.

Pages 4, 7-8 describe Iranian oil and weapons-procurement networks routing cargo through intermediary hubs (Southeast Asia) with ship-to-ship transfers, AIS manipulation, and forged documents relabeling Iranian oil as 'Malaysian blend' before it reaches China; weapons procurement networks are also said to use 'transshipping through third countries' to obscure Iran as end user (p.7). This matches SAN003's mechanism of re-papering cargo at an intermediary hub so the sanctioned leg is hidden, distinct from SAN006's invoice-mispricing/misdescription mechanism already claimed.

Page 8 red flag: transactions 'move through multiple exchange houses and/or trading companies, adding additional fees and costs as the transactions progress' where volume/pattern don't match customary practice, and page 5 notes front-company accounts let sanctioned entities transact 'without ever repatriating funds to Iran.' This matches BA008's layering mechanism of pushing funds through a chain of intermediary hops to sever the audit trail before reaching an identifiable destination, a correspondent-banking-family technique distinct from the sanctions-family typologies already claimed.

Page 9 red flag: 'Multiple companies incorporated at roughly the same time share counterparties, addresses, owners, or name similarities and demonstrate similar transaction profiles'; page 5 notes indications of Iranian control include 'shared counterparties, addresses, and name similarities'; the p.6 Zarringhalam case study describes a 'sprawling network of front companies' across the UAE and Hong Kong. This matches PAT007's network-level mechanism (shared directors/addresses/beneficial owners forming an identifiable shell network) as distinct from SAN004's single-entity front-company attributes already claimed.

Page 10 red flag: 'Incoming transactions from many unrelated wallets in relatively small amounts (accumulation of funds) with subsequent transfer to another wallet or full exchange for fiat currency.' This is the funnel-account pattern -- many small, unrelated depositors aggregating into one collection point that then clears onward -- applied to VA wallets instead of bank accounts.

Pages 7-8 develop a velocity-specific pattern distinct from the already-claimed BA008 Layering (which is about hop-count/opacity, not speed): 'multiple high-value transactions...in short succession, such as within a 24-hour period' and depositing VAs then 'immediately withdrawing/converting...This effectively turns the exchange/VASP into an ML mixer.' Case Study 4 (page 11) evidences two USD 4.8m transactions six minutes apart. The mechanism matches BA005's 'funds land on an account and clear back out again almost immediately... defined by HOW FAST funds move.'

Case Study 1 (page 8): 'the individuals shared the same residential address...indicating the potential use of money mules by professional money launderers.' PAT005 Common Address 'identifies entities connected through a shared address' -- here the shared residential address is the evidentiary link tying more than 150 seemingly separate mule identities together as one professional laundering network.

Page 7-8 red flag lists high-value transactions directed 'to a newly created or to a previously inactive account' as suspicious. This matches BA006 Dormant Reactivation's core signal of an idle account suddenly receiving flows disproportionate to its history, though the advisory gives only a single embedded clause rather than a developed case, hence low confidence.

Page 21 fronting red flags ('Inconsistencies in name spellings or transliterations, particularly those stemming from Cyrillic spellings' and 'Frequent or unexplained changes of name or declared location of operation') describe defeat of list-based name screening through transliteration/alias variance -- the exact mechanism SAN005 names -- distinct from the already-claimed ownership/front-company typologies which concern structural concealment, not name-form evasion.

Page 26 intermediary-country risk table lists, as a standalone country-level risk activity for BVI and Republic of Cyprus, 'Use of complex corporate structures such as trust arrangements or complex corporate structures involving offshore companies' -- flagged without reference to any specific designated person. This matches SAN009's distinguishing feature that opacity itself, not resolution to a named DP, is the finding, separate from the DP-specific ownership chains already claimed under SAN001.

emergent_label: Alternative Financial Messaging System Exposure (SPFS)
rationale: Page 11: 'OFSI encourages UK banks to assess their exposure to institutions who have joined the System for Transfer of Financial Messages (SPFS). Designed by the Central Bank of Russia as an alternative to SWIFT, SPFS could be used to breach UK financial sanctions prohibitions.' No correspondent-banking typology in the library (BA001-BA010) covers evasion via a parallel, sanctioned-state-built payment messaging network replacing SWIFT; search returned no match, so this is proposed as emergent.

Document repeatedly evidences settlement/payment being routed through a party other than the trade counterparty, breaking the trade-funds link: 2.12 flags 'orders from unconnected third parties'; 2.35-2.38 discuss 'non-standard settlement' where a customer directs delivery to an account held with a third-party broker, and note participants mitigating 'third-party payments and third-party transfers of assets' seen in the Deutsche Bank case; the Annex red-flag list (p.19) separately lists 'instructions or involvement from third parties'; Example 7b (p.29) has cash withdrawn 'to a third-party account'. This matches TBML008's mechanism of a payer/recipient who is not the trade counterparty obscuring the true source/destination of funds.

emergent_label: Discounted Convertible Equity Issuance Wash
rationale: Example 4 (pp.25-26): a small-cap issuer, majority offshore-owned, issues a convertible bond to an undisclosed connected investor, who converts £100,000 debt into £1,000,000 of shares (10x market discount) 30 days later, sells the shares, and repatriates cash to a UK account. FCA concludes (para 22-23) the activity 'wash[ed] illicit funds through the markets... by lending money to the company, which was exchanged for shares that can be sold for more than the value of the loan,' and notes debt need not even be issued -- only new shares transferred to connected parties for sale. Distinct from claimed MTN/debt-issuance layering (cross-border coupon remittance via offshore agent) and generic Related Party Trading (only flags the connection, not the mispriced-issuance-and-dump mechanism).

emergent_label: Trade Value Offsetting for Terrorist Proxy Financing
rationale: Page 35 describes a November 2018 OFAC action against Iranian and Russian entities that used 'a payment offsetting arrangement in which the sale and shipment of Iranian oil to Syria provided hundreds of millions of dollars to Iran's terror proxy groups, including Hizballah, HAMAS, and the IRGC-QF.' This is not vessel-identity deception, transshipment, ownership opacity, or trade mispricing (SAN002/SAN003/SAN006/SAN009) -- it is the use of the trade settlement mechanism itself (offsetting rather than cash payment) to generate and channel value directly to designated terrorist organizations. No existing typology in the library (sanctions, TBML, or otherwise) captures value-transfer-via-trade-offset as a terrorist-financing mechanism; search returned no match above the score floor. Proposing as a single, low-confidence emergent typology since the advisory only describes one case study and does not develop it into a full indicator set.

Section IV / Box 2 (pp.21,23 of PDF; printed 19,21) explicitly describes the cash-controller network depositing illicit cash 'in amounts under the reporting threshold to avoid detection' and, in the worked example, the collector delivers cash to a complicit transmitter to place into bank accounts, visiting three different branches to 'structure the deposits into the account' before the controller directs onward transfer to settle accounts abroad. This matches BA001's mechanism of sub-threshold, multi-branch deposits followed by onward wiring to a single beneficiary.
