Box 20 (p.43 of PDF; printed 41) describes fraud victims being 'instructed to wire money into funnel accounts held by other co-conspirators (money mules), who then quickly transferred the money to other US accounts as well as accounts around the world before victims could discover the fraud', with one mule opening 38 fraudulent bank accounts. This matches BA002's mechanism of a collection account receiving many dispersed deposits and rapidly clearing them onward to a downstream beneficiary before the pattern is reviewed, distinct from the single pass-through BA003 Mule Accounts already claimed.

Box 2.6 (p.24) describes an OCG that 'registered and used legal entities and established a fake paper trail for sales and purchases to create value-added tax chains' to both disguise proceeds and generate additional criminal proceeds -- a classic VAT-chain/round-tripping structure matching TBML006's closed-loop, related-party trade mechanism. Evidence is a single sentence within a broader case study, so confidence is low.

emergent_label: Gold/Precious Metals as Cash Proxy (Commodity-for-Cash Value Transfer)
rationale: P.21 states gold's exploitation includes its use 'as an alternative form of value within the ML process -- i.e. not just a commodity to exploit in moving value, but also a proxy for cash.' Box 2.5 (p.23) develops this: Peruvian nationals purchased criminally-derived gold and sold it to complicit U.S. refineries who 'completed the ML cycle' by paying via wire transfers disguised as legitimate wholesale purchases. Unlike TBML001-005 (document/price misrepresentation) or BMPE (currency-exchange broker chain), here the commodity itself functions directly as a cash-equivalent settled through an ordinary sale to a complicit counterparty, with no misrepresentation of the trade documents. No existing Knowledge Centre typology matched this mechanism on search.

Footnote 11 (p.14) describes procurement of 'logistical equipment and weaponizable technology such as used vehicles or drones to conflict zones' as a TBTF sub-typology -- civilian-use goods diverted to a military end-use via ordinary trade. This is TBML007's twin of SAN007 Dual Use Goods, but the convention prefers the sanctions twin only when the advisory is framed as sanctions/export-control evasion. This report is framed entirely as TBML/TBTF (trade-based money laundering and terrorist financing), with no sanctions-regime or designated-party framing in the passage, so the TBML twin fits the document's own framing. Single footnote, not elaborated, so confidence is low.

Doctrine: payment settles a trade through a payer who is not the trade counterparty, breaking the link between trade and funds. Brazil case (p.32, Box 3.3): hairdressers received/transferred funds and were invoiced by miners 'for importing on their behalf', while the actual miners were compensated separately 'through a network of underground exchange market dealers' rather than directly by the Southeast Asian buyers. Congo/Rwanda gold case (p.22): 'The payment would then be made either by the intermediary to the smuggler, or would come later once the intermediary got the gold to a refiner' -- payer is not the original trade counterparty. Chapter highlight (p.33) explicitly cites 'integrating proceeds through third party wire transfers under the guise of payments for goods and services'.

Doctrine: over-invoicing inflates the price of goods intentionally beyond true market value. Advisory p.31 states explicitly that criminals 'over or under declare goods being shipped' as a common TBML thread; Annex A (p.58) describes the specific mechanism: timber/gold 'exported at below market prices, change ownership and Bill of Lading en route... and is imported at recipient countries at higher declared values' -- an explicit over-declaration of value at the import leg to launder the price differential, distinct from the already-claimed under-invoicing (TBML002U) which covers the export-side under-declaration only.

Doctrine: Hidden Controller identifies individuals exercising effective control despite not appearing as declared owner/director, evidenced by nominee director structures and concealed ownership arrangements. This advisory develops the mechanism across three independent findings: p.19 'These PEPs will often act as... nominee directors of corporations'; p.22 'the named individual on the registry would be a nominee with only a loose connection to the ultimate underlying owner'; and the Box 4.10 case (p.47) where financial analysis 'facilitated the identification of the network and the nominees used to disguise the beneficial ownership of bank accounts and front companies'. This is control-without-ownership via nominee arrangement, matching PAT010 specifically rather than the already-claimed PAT007 shell-network structure.

Doctrine: layering pushes placed funds through a chain of transfers to sever the audit trail, putting distance/opacity between the seed account and destination, with no obligation to close a loop (distinguishing it from circular flows). Advisory p.23 describes exactly this: as large banks de-risk and smaller/regional institutions step in, this creates 'additional layers between the originator and the beneficiary,' and 'nesting the activity within a correspondent banking relationship obscures the ultimate beneficial owner and decreases the risk of transactions associated with environmental crime being identified.'

emergent_label: Informal Value Transfer (Hawala) Networks for Environmental Crime Proceeds
rationale: No existing typology matches this mechanism (best search score 0.36, against Under Invoicing). The advisory describes a distinct movement technique: p.22, gold smuggled from DRC onward to Asia relies on 'informal remittance networks such as hawalas, in an effort to avoid the scrutiny of the formal financial sector'; p.31 chapter finding confirms 'the important role of underground money value transfer services (MVTS) to facilitate laundering from environmental crimes, and particularly illegal mining... reflect local informal transfer systems (e.g., hawala)'. This is a specific channel for moving illicit value outside formal banking rails, distinct from the already-claimed cash-intensive-business typology (BA007), warranting its own emergent entry pending Knowledge Centre review.

Paras 26-29 (p.22) and the asset-recovery discussion (p.44, p.49-50) describe CEF-proceeds being rapidly layered through 'pass-through' transactions and account hopping across multiple FIs/PSPs/remitters, with funds clearing almost immediately and law enforcement needing to intervene within 24-72 hours before dissipation. This matches BA005's velocity-defined mechanism (funds landing and clearing out almost immediately, throughput multiples of normal activity) rather than generic mule/shell typologies already claimed.

Para 29 (p.22) explicitly names 'smurfing' as a CEF ML evasion technique, and Box 17 France PSP case (p.30) describes criminals 'splitting the amounts between several accounts' specifically to stay under the PSP's cash withdrawal limits and internal monitoring threshold. This is the break-amounts-into-pieces-to-stay-under-a-reporting/monitoring-threshold mechanism BA001 Structuring describes, applied to PSP thresholds rather than a CTR line.

Para 24 (p.19) and Box 9 Turkiye case (p.20) describe CEF-controlled shell companies opening 'virtual point-of-sale accounts with merchant services companies' to receive victim payments -- 135 shell companies processed TRY 9.6bn of fraud proceeds this way. This matches BA009's mechanism of a merchant/card-processing relationship boarded against a declared business being used as an undisclosed processing front for volume the acquirer never screened.

emergent_label: Underground Banking / Hawala Remittance for CEF Proceeds
rationale: No KC typology cleared the search floor for hawala/unlicensed remitters. Para 30 (p.25) names 'underground money remitters or hawala services with little or no AML/CFT controls' as a distinct CEF ML technique for moving proceeds out of jurisdiction, and Box 14 Japan case (p.26) shows funds physically routed 'to Ghana through an underground bank linked to the Ghanaian community in Japan' as one of three parallel laundering channels. This is a distinct informal-value-transfer mechanism not covered by the shell company, mule or TBML typologies already claimed.

emergent_label: Synthetic/Stolen Identity Accounts for Direct Criminal Control
rationale: No KC typology cleared the search floor for synthetic/stolen identity account creation. Para 35 (p.27) describes criminals using stolen or synthetic identities to 'directly set up and control accounts' such that 'the account holders may not even be aware of their involvement,' and Box 16 Austria (p.28) develops this: VASP accounts were opened in victims' names without their knowledge via remote access tools and used directly by criminals for laundering. This differs from BA003 Mule Accounts (already claimed), which involves a real, if deceived or complicit, account holder acting on a controller's instruction -- here no consenting or duped natural person is involved at all; the identity itself is fabricated or stolen at account opening.

Box 3 (India, p.26) describes a scheme where 'the network also used circular trade flows. Goods were exported to related entities in a third jurisdiction, where payment was deliberately withheld on the basis of fictitious commercial disputes, before the goods were re-exported to entities controlled by the same network' -- a closed loop of goods/value returning to related parties with no genuine change of ownership, matching TBML006's core mechanism. This is a distinct settlement typology from the already-claimed TBML001/TBML002U/TBML009.

Para 71(ii), p.25 lists 'phantom shipments' as a named trade-based settlement mechanism used by underground bankers/HOSSPs to balance inter-operator accounts via fictitious trade transactions -- i.e. invoices/payments justified without genuine movement of goods, matching TBML004's mechanism. Evidence is a single named bullet rather than a developed case, hence medium confidence.

Para 71(ii), p.25 states underground bankers/HOSSPs 'manipulate invoices—through over- or under-invoicing and falsified cargo descriptions—to balance inter-operator accounts via fictitious trade transactions,' explicitly naming misdescription of the shipped commodity as a distinct mechanism from over/under-invoicing (already claimed), matching TBML005's declared-vs-actual-goods mechanism.

Paras 74-75 (p.26-27) describe: 'Third party money mules are commonly used to fragment large-sum criminal cash into multiple small deposits and transfer them to designated accounts, avoiding the AML monitoring thresholds of FIs,' and cuckoo smurfing where 'structured cash deposits are used to balance domestic payouts.' This matches BA001's doctrine mechanism of 'deliberate breaking-up of cash deposits into amounts... to keep individual deposits below the reporting trigger.' Distinct from the already-claimed BA003 Mule Accounts, which concerns the mule-account layer rather than the deposit-structuring technique itself.

Para 71(ii) (p.25) notes trade-front companies 'typically operating in cash-intensive sectors (e.g. vehicle sales or luxury goods), often exhibit frequent cash deposits,' and Box 4 (Germany, p.27) describes 'cash-intensive businesses, such as kiosks, hookah bars, mobile phone shops or souvenir shops' providing 'cover for cash deposits, third-party payments, and mixed funding sources.' This matches BA007's doctrine of a cash-intensive business used as 'a legitimate cover for laundering physical cash' with deposits disproportionate to the declared business profile.

Box 6 (Japan, p.29) describes automated transfer tools 'configured to move funds from mule, third-party, or compromised accounts once deposits reach a specified amount,' with threshold-triggered 'sweeping' that helps 'move funds rapidly through multiple accounts, reducing the time proceeds remain in any single account.' This matches BA005's doctrine that funds 'land on an account and clear back out again almost immediately, resting only long enough to register a balance change before they are gone.'

Doc defines 'Unexplained Third Party' (p.31 glossary) and lists as a DC red flag 'Unexplained third parties' in document discrepancies (p.45) and 'Third parties are funding or part funding the DC value (just in time account credits to the settlement account)' under repayment arrangements for both DCs (p.45) and BCs (p.57). Bank A/B are also instructed to screen any bank/party receiving payment that was not part of the original DC (p.40). This matches TBML008's mechanism of settlement via a payer who is not the trade counterparty, breaking the link between trade and funds.

Core Principles Paper explicitly states that trade-based misrepresentation of value 'generally rel[ies] upon collusion between the seller and buyer' and that 'collusion may arise because both parties are controlled by the same persons' (p.12). This is operationalised in the DC risk indicator table as 'Connected applicant and beneficiary' (p.45) and in the BC risk indicator table as 'Connected Drawer or Drawee' (p.57), matching PAT009's mechanism of trading activity between entities connected through ownership or control.

emergent_label: Fraudulent Claims Under Standby/Guarantee Instruments
rationale: Appendix III (p.59-67) explains that unlike DCs, Guarantees and SBLCs are non-performance instruments where 'payments would generally be the exception' (p.60), and then lists a dedicated risk-indicator group for claims/payment instructions: 'Claims made within a short time after issuance', 'Continuous claims under various guarantee instruments' and 'Claim pressure tactics' (p.67). No existing typology in the library (searched, no match above floor) captures abuse of the demand/claim mechanism of standby instruments to extract payment absent genuine non-performance -- distinct from TBML documentary-fraud typologies which concern misrepresented goods/invoices rather than fraudulent invocation of a payment-on-default instrument.

Page 25 describes criminals using cash-intensive businesses (restaurants, hotels, car washes) to mix illicit funds with the businesses' legitimate income -- the exact placement mechanism BA007 Cash Intensive Activity doctrine defines as cash disproportionate to a declared business profile used as cover for laundering. Not already covered by the claimed TBML/SAN/CMI/emergent typologies, which address trade-based sanctions evasion, front companies, crypto and corruption/hybrid proxies, not cash-business placement.

Pages 25 and 33 describe young and vulnerable recruits, sourced via social media and gaming platforms, acting as money mules who receive and transfer illicit funds through their own bank accounts in exchange for a small cut -- matching BA003 Mule Accounts' mechanism of a personal account used as a pass-through, moving money at a controller's instruction while retaining little for itself. This is distinct from the already-claimed crypto layering, corruption-broker and hybrid-proxy typologies, none of which address personal bank-account muling.

emergent_label: VAT Missing Trader / Carousel and Contra-Trading Fraud (MTIC)
rationale: Pages 75-76 develop, in detail, the missing-trader mechanism (a trader imports goods VAT-free, charges VAT domestically, then disappears without remitting it), carousel fraud (the same goods repeatedly imported/exported across Member States to claim false VAT refunds), and the more complex contra-trading variant (an extra layer of companies creating a second trading circuit), illustrated by a EUR 297 million/400-company case example. No existing Knowledge Centre typology (search returned no match above floor) captures this specific VAT-refund exploitation mechanism; it is distinct from the claimed TBML/SAN/CMI typologies which concern trade-value manipulation for sanctions/laundering rather than VAT-refund fraud via missing traders.

emergent_label: Hawala and Informal Value Transfer Systems (IVTS) for Illicit Proceeds
rationale: Page 24 lists 'informal value transfer systems' alongside cash businesses, shell-company layering and cryptocurrency as core components of the parallel financial criminal underworld, and the page 52 migrant-smuggling case example shows irregular migrants paying smuggling fees 'directly to hawala offices, also in cryptocurrencies.' This is a distinct value-movement mechanism (informal, non-bank remittance networks) not addressed by the claimed sanctions/TBML/crypto typologies. Search returned no matching existing typology above the floor.
